content:
Yesterday saw two conflicting reports about next year's new model celebrating the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, said to embody Apple's long-standing vision of "a single slab of glass."

There have been conflicting reports before about what we will actually see, but yesterday's divergence was the biggest yet…

Current situation

Former Apple design chief Jony Ive often spoke of his long-term vision for the iPhone as one that would eventually become a single sheet of glass. It is widely believed that even though Ive has left, Apple still holds onto this vision.

While Apple doesn't generally make a big deal of product anniversaries, the prevailing view is that they are aiming to realise this vision as much as possible at the iPhone's 20th anniversary. This will very likely include embedding Face ID under the display, and possibly hiding the front camera beneath the screen as well.

However, we have already seen several conflicting reports. Although the initial assumption was that it would be a standalone model, similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, more recent reports have suggested that this design will instead appear on next year's iPhone Pro models.

In order, that should be the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple may skip that name to celebrate the anniversary and jump straight to the iPhone 20.

Yesterday's conflicting reports

Yesterday things got even more muddled when an analyst claimed that Apple had abandoned the idea of an all-glass iPhone next year.

However, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman quickly stepped in to refute this claim.

What is more likely

The point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone is not a single endpoint. Whatever Apple plans to release next year, it is only one step, or a few steps, towards that sci-fi "single sheet of glass" vision.

The question is not whether that goal can be reached next year, but how far Apple will move towards that vision. But whether it is one step or several, this will certainly not be the last step in the evolution of the iPhone's design.

In fact, Gurman says Apple has already made compromises on what it had originally hoped to achieve next year.

Jefferies' analyst most likely heard the same news, but being closer to the source, interpreted it as Apple having completely abandoned the plan.

My own expectation is that next year's design will be a major advance – comparable to the big leap of the iPhone X – but with further developments to come in the years after. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will move forward enough to allow Apple to adopt some kind of special branding, whether that means labelling it as a 20th anniversary iPhone (which I think is unlikely), using some other special name, or skipping a generation and calling it the iPhone 20.

What are your expectations? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments.
